summary: The developer machine has the essential runtime, the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server, and the DocumentDB agent skills needed to build the Python LlamaIndex provider-directory vector-search sample. Most cold answers were verified and corrected against Microsoft Learn pages — the main confusions arise from mixing older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) concepts and Atlas-style Mongo syntaxes with the current Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters + cosmosSearch) model. Missing CLI tools (mongosh, bicep, terraform, azd) and an unspecified embedding-provider/env-var choice are workable gaps but not showstoppers for the Python sample running against the provided cluster.
summary_points: Build can start: Python, pip, Node, az, Docker, the documentdb MCP server and the documentdb-* skills needed are available.

Several cold answers were incorrect: resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts); vector indexes use the cosmosSearch/createIndexes APIs (vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann), not Atlas 'knnVector' syntax; Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) auth is supported when enabled.
Vector search and index creation docs are available and were used to ground the correct index shapes and query patterns (cosmosSearch operator, vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann).
Missing but non-blocking tools: mongosh, bicep, terraform, azd; add mongosh to improve manual verification; IaC tooling is optional because run environment forbids provisioning.

Information gaps remain: embedding model/provider and env var for its credentials, and small decisions (index dims, index method choice) that the builder must pick and document before running the seed/index script.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account-level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for MongoDB-compatible accounts). Example ARM/Bicep resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore-style, MongoDB-compatible clusters the current ARM/Bicep resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the mongoClusters resource). The Azure templates and AVM modules show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters as the cluster-level resource to deploy a Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) cluster.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2023-11-15-preview (deployment-language-arm-template)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB and its 'databaseAccounts' resource covered many APIs (including older MongoDB API accounts). The model changed: new vCore MongoDB clusters are exposed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters. The shared 'Microsoft.DocumentDB' provider namespace and earlier 'databaseAccounts' pages cause the mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts instead of mongoClusters for IaC or lookup paths, IaC templates or CLI calls would target the wrong resource type; automation that expects a databaseAccounts-style account would fail to find cluster-specific properties (shard/cluster options).
improvements: On the main 'Create cluster' and Quickstart pages, add one explicit sentence: 'For MongoDB vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts).' and link to the mongoClusters template.
Add a short deprecation/clarification banner to the older databaseAccounts docs that points readers to mongoClusters for vCore MongoDB clusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example commands: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB; az cosmosdb show --name myAccount --resource-group myRg. This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb) rather than a separate extension.
confusions.grounded_answer: There are dedicated command groups for Mongo clusters: az documentdb mongocluster and az cosmosdb mongocluster exist (CLI references show az documentdb mongocluster create and az cosmosdb mongocluster create). The az CLI exposes both command groups (documentdb extension/commands and cosmosdb command group may host mongocluster subcommands); builders should use the 'az documentdb mongocluster' group when following DocumentDB-specific guidance and ensure the documentdb CLI extension is installed/available.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
az cosmosdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'az cosmosdb' group historically manages Cosmos databaseAccounts; newer vCore/mongoClusters commands appear under both 'az cosmosdb' and the 'documentdb' command set (preview/extensions) which creates ambiguity. The cold answer assumed only the classic az cosmosdb group.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong CLI group might produce commands that don't support cluster-specific options (authAllowedModes, server-version, shard options), leading to failing CLI scripts or incorrect parameters.
improvements: Document the preferred CLI command group in the quickstart: e.g., 'For vCore mongoClusters prefer az documentdb mongocluster create; if az cosmosdb mongocluster exists in your CLI, it is an alias/extension—check az version and installed extensions.'
Add an 'az module/extension check' snippet to the DocumentDB quickstart to show the exact az extension needed.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Example Bicep: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }. Terraform (AzureRM): azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For MongoDB vCore clusters the current Bicep/ARM resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples and AVM modules target this resource). databaseAccounts remains the resource type for Cosmos DB database accounts (API-for-NoSQL and other APIs), but vCore-style mongo clusters use the mongoClusters resource type in ARM/Bicep and (AzAPI/AzureRM) Terraform modules.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB historically published databaseAccounts as the main resource. The newer vCore MongoDB clusters are a separate resource type (mongoClusters) in the same provider namespace, which is an easy namespace/shape confusion.
confusions.build_risk: IaC templates targeting databaseAccounts may not surface cluster-specific properties or may attempt to create a different kind of account; deployments or preflight checks in CI may fail.
improvements: Add a clear example Bicep snippet to the DocumentDB quickstart that shows 'resource mongoCluster Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@<api>' so builders copy the correct resource shape.
Add a brief 'Which resource to use' decision box to the IaC docs differentiating databaseAccounts vs mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-compatible connection string for Azure DocumentDB (Cosmos DB Mongo API): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<accountName>@. For SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. TLS/SSL must be enabled (ssl=true); port for non-SRV TLS connections is 10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: Connection strings vary by cluster type and endpoint naming: current Azure DocumentDB/Mongo clusters often use SRV endpoints like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (mongodb+srv) with TLS and authMechanism settings; older Cosmos DB API-for-Mongo endpoints used *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com or *.documents.azure.com and port 10255. The practical guidance: use the connection string returned by the portal/az CLI (copy to DOCUMENTDB_URI), ensure tls/tlsAllowInvalidCertificates options for local dev, and use mongodb+srv where supported. Do not rely on a single hard-coded host suffix/port for every cluster.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple, overlapping endpoint formats exist across older Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts and the newer DocumentDB/mongoClusters endpoints (SRV forms like mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com); the cold answer mixed the older cosmos host naming and parameters.

confusion_sources.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.build_risk: Hard-coding the wrong host suffix/port can cause connection failures or TLS misconfigurations. The safe approach is to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from environment and use the portal/az-provided connection string.
improvements: In the quickstart and sample README, instruct builders to copy the exact connection string from the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings and store it in DOCUMENTDB_URI (example command snippet).
Add a short 'Connection string formats' table showing SRV vs non-SRV examples and when to use tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local dev.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: There are multiple provisioning models: traditional Cosmos billing by Request Units (RU/s) (provisioned throughput or autoscale), a serverless option for some workloads, and newer vCore-based dedicated compute SKUs for MongoDB-compatible clusters (vCore tiers like M-series). Depending on the account SKU you will be billed by RU/s or by vCore allocation. (Expect to choose either RU/s or a vCore compute tier when creating the account.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure Cosmos DB supports multiple capacity/billing models. For MongoDB-compatible workloads you can have RU-based provisioned throughput (and serverless for certain account types) or the vCore-based dedicated compute SKUs (the vCore/M-series clusters). Use the Azure cost docs and the Cost Estimator to pick the right mode.

grounding_links.title: Plan and manage costs for Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary data-plane auth for MongoDB-compatible accounts is username/password using the account keys (the connection string contains the username and primary/secondary key as password) and standard MongoDB SCRAM auth. Historically Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) authentication is not supported for MongoDB wire protocol data connections; Entra ID is used for management/RBAC via ARM but not as a driver auth mechanism for the MongoDB API. Use the provided connection string/primary key for drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: This is incorrect: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (username/password) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) authentication for data-plane access when MicrosoftEntraID is enabled on the cluster (authConfig.allowedModes). The service documents how to enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication and how to connect using OIDC (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and special authMechanismProperties in the connection string).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older or partial docs and the historic focus on connection-string credentials (username/primary-key) led to an assumption that Entra ID isn't supported for the MongoDB wire protocol. The product now documents OIDC support explicitly.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes Entra ID isn't supported, they may fail to implement recommended RBAC or may embed long-lived credentials in env vars rather than enabling Entra/OIDC flows where appropriate.
improvements: Add a prominent example in the quickstart showing how to turn on MicrosoftEntraID in authConfig and a sample connection string for OIDC (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC...).
On the 'Connect' docs, add a short troubleshooting note: 'If you only see username/password examples, consider enabling MicrosoftEntraID in authConfig to use OIDC.'

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for the data plane. For Python, use pymongo (pip install pymongo). There is no special service-specific data-plane SDK for Mongo operations; Azure provides management SDKs (Azure SDK for Python) for provisioning and ARM operations but for database access use the official MongoDB driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documented guidance is to use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for data-plane operations. Management/provisioning uses Azure control-plane SDKs/CLI.

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Vector indexes on Mongo-compatible DocumentDB are typically created using MongoDB-style kNN vector indexes (e.g., knnVector) and can use algorithms like HNSW (or DiskANN/IVF on some SKUs). Example createIndex command (Mongo shell / pymongo): db.providers.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } } ) — adjust dimensions and method params for your embeddings. (This is the shape of the command you should issue.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, and vector-diskann (with product quantization / half-precision options) and creates them using the service's createIndexes / createSearchIndexes patterns and the 'cosmosSearch' index operator; queries use the $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator. The index definition shape uses cosmosSearchOptions with kind (vector-hnsw/vector-ivf/vector-diskann), dimensions, similarity, and algorithm-specific parameters (m, efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, etc.).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB
Vector search quickstarts and index examples

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used Atlas-style knnVector createIndex syntax. Azure DocumentDB exposes its own vector index creation semantics (cosmosSearchOptions, index kinds vector-hnsw/ivf/diskann) and uses the cosmosSearch operator in $search.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues Atlas-style createIndex commands (knnVector) the service will reject them or create an incompatible index; vector queries would fail. The correct API must be used (createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions or the createSearchIndexes tooling).
improvements: Replace any Atlas createIndex examples in the agent guidance with DocumentDB cosmosSearch createIndexes JSON examples (include one HNSW and one DiskANN example) in the Vector Search quickstart.

Add a short conversion note: 'If you copy Atlas/knnVector syntax, replace it with cosmosSearchOptions { kind: "vector-hnsw" | "vector-ivf" | "vector-diskann" } and call the $search stage with cosmosSearch operator.'

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text/search functionality is done either via the MongoDB "search" (Atlas Search style) aggregation stage ($search) if the service exposes Atlas-like search indexes, or by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search for Cosmos DB accounts when you need richer hybrid queries. Hybrid vector+text ranking is typically done with a combined query stage that uses the vector index for nearest-neighbors plus text predicates/boosting (e.g., a compound $search with vector and text clauses or an application-side hybrid ranker that combines cosine scores with text match scores).
confusions.grounded_answer: Current Azure DocumentDB provides native full-text and vector search via its integrated vector/text search: you create search indexes (cosmosSearchOptions) and use the $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator, which supports combining lexical and vector clauses. You can also integrate with external Azure Cognitive Search for other scenarios, but DocumentDB supports hybrid (vector + text) queries directly via $search/cosmosSearch.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer correctly named $search but suggested Atlas-specific expectations and an external search integration as the primary route; DocumentDB implements $search/cosmosSearch natively and supports hybrid searches without requiring Azure Cognitive Search.
confusions.build_risk: If builders look for Atlas Search tooling or attempt to pipe data to Cognitive Search by default, they may add needless complexity and extra services; using $search/cosmosSearch yields an easier, single-store hybrid approach.
improvements: On the Vector Search quickstart, add a short recipe: 'To combine vector and text filters, use the $search stage with cosmosSearch and include vector and text clauses; sample JSON provided.'
Remove Atlas-specific examples from sample repos and replace them with cosmosSearch examples.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported wire protocol/server versions depend on the account SKU; recent offerings support MongoDB 6.0 and 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Some MongoDB features historically missing or different include server-side JavaScript, some aggregation stages or operators, and certain transaction/replica-set behaviors — always test your workload. Expect most common CRUD, aggregation, and driver APIs to work but verify advanced features (e.g. DB-level users, some admin commands) in your cluster.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB documents that it supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (product docs list support across these versions) and implements 99.03% of MongoDB query/aggregation operators. A small set of administrative commands and a few operators may differ; run the compatibility assessment for migration.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged on versions; official docs list the supported wire protocol ranges explicitly. The product evolves and now documents support for 5.0–8.0 in the compatibility pages.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming an unsupported wire version could cause driver incompatibilities; conversely, assuming old limitations may cause unnecessary refactors. Run tests against the target cluster's advertised server/version.
improvements: Add an explicit 'supported wire protocol versions' note to the quickstart and compatibility pages with the latest supported versions to reduce guesswork.
Include a small snippet to check server wire version from a driver (e.g., client.server_info()) in the quickstart so builders can confirm at runtime.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator that replicates the Azure DocumentDB Mongo API feature set. For local development run a vanilla MongoDB Docker image (for feature parity pick the same server version the cluster advertises, e.g. mongo:7.0) and bind to the standard port 27017: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name local-mongo -d mongo:7.0. Use this for local integration tests, but validate against the real cluster for Azure-specific behaviors (indexes/knn algorithms).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a local DocumentDB gateway/container image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) and a documented local development loop with gateway endpoint published at port 10260 by convention. The official local gateway is preferred for reproducing DocumentDB-specific behavior (gateway TLS and DocumentDB vector/index features) rather than a vanilla mongo: container on 27017.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: start DocumentDB in a Docker container

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed generic MongoDB local dev practice (mongo:27017). DocumentDB provides an official local gateway image and a recommended port (10260) for parity with the service.
confusions.build_risk: Using mongo:latest locally will miss DocumentDB-specific behavior (cosmosSearch vector indexes, DiskANN/HNSW features and portal/cluster-specific auth modes) and produce misleading test outcomes.
improvements: In local-deployment guidance, emphasize the recommended DocumentDB gateway Docker image and port 10260 and provide the exact docker run command.
Add a short matrix showing which DocumentDB features the local gateway supports vs which are only in cloud clusters.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams (watch) are supported when the cluster exposes a replica-set/oplog and the Mongo wire-protocol compatibility level includes change-stream support (newer MongoDB-compatible clusters do). Typically no additional per-collection flag is required, but the account/cluster SKU must support change streams; ensure the user has the needed privileges and test watch() on the target collection. If change streams are not supported on your SKU you will get an error.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. For typical single-shard clusters no extra steps are required, but for multishard clusters certain preview/enabling steps (feature toggle) may be required; docs show how to enable change-stream features for multishard clusters and describe resume tokens, historical checkpoints, and retention guidance. Builders should follow the 'Change streams in Azure DocumentDB' guidance when using them in production or for online migrations.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was broadly right but omitted the specific scenario where multishard clusters require an opt-in/preview feature or 'enable change streams for multishard clusters' steps.
confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes change streams are always enabled on every cluster, migration or real-time features may fail on multishard clusters until the feature is enabled.
improvements: Add an explicit 'enable change streams for multishard clusters' note in the change-streams quickstart and mention the portal/CLI steps to toggle it.
Provide a small code snippet that shows checking change stream availability and handling the error message when change streams are disallowed.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server for data-plane inspection/agent tools for Azure DocumentDB (Mongo-compatible); the general Azure MCP server does not expose the service-specific documentdb data-plane inspection tools. The prompt indicates a documentdb MCP server with profile 'default' is provided — use that.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list/create indexes, run aggregates, explain, sample documents). The general Azure MCP server covers control-plane and cross-service lookups but not the detailed DocumentDB data-plane surface.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb MCP server (inventory) and Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit docs

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB MCP Toolkit

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally used the name DocumentDB for the original Cosmos DB (SQL) service; Cosmos DB superseded DocumentDB. Azure "DocumentDB" historically referred to what is now Azure Cosmos DB. The open-source "DocumentDB" projects (if any) are unrelated; Azure's DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a proprietary Microsoft service that offers multiple APIs (SQL, MongoDB-compatible, Cassandra-compatible, Gremlin, Table).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly right but confusing: historically 'DocumentDB' was the name of the original Cosmos DB SQL API service; Cosmos DB evolved from DocumentDB. The current product 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' refers to the managed MongoDB-compatible database built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB engine project). The open-source DocumentDB engine exists and is the upstream for the managed service; the naming overlap causes confusion with Azure Cosmos DB and with other vendors' 'DocumentDB' names (e.g., Amazon's DocumentDB).

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical rebrandings (DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB) plus the reuse of 'DocumentDB' as a product name for the new managed Mongo-compatible service and an open-source engine lead to ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: If builders follow old 'Cosmos DB DocumentDB' instructions they may target the wrong API surface (databaseAccounts) or expect different features; naming confusion can lead to wrong IaC or CLI usage.
improvements: Add a short 'Names and lineage' section to top-level docs that explicitly maps: 'DocumentDB (original) -> Cosmos DB; Azure DocumentDB (current) = managed Mongo-compatible service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; do not confuse with Amazon DocumentDB or Cosmos DB databaseAccounts.'
Add cross-links between the open-source DocumentDB repo README and the Azure product overview to make lineage explicit.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Microsoft Azure's Cosmos DB storage/engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol (it is not a stock mongod process). In practice you use standard MongoDB drivers, but expect some behavioral differences and missing admin features; thoroughly test your workload. Use the MongoDB driver APIs unchanged but validate behavior against the platform.
confusions.grounded_answer: The managed Azure DocumentDB Mongo-compatible service is implemented on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) rather than a stock mongod. Applications use standard MongoDB drivers without code changes in most cases, but there are platform-specific behaviors and admin commands that differ. The important point: use MongoDB drivers but test for small compatibility differences; the core engine is DocumentDB (open-source), not the upstream MongoDB server.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed a Cosmos DB storage engine implementation; the product documentation explicitly explains the open-source DocumentDB engine underlies the service and is not a stock mongod process.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming the underlying engine is the same as Cosmos DB's NoSQL engine or a stock mongod could cause wrong assumptions about admin commands, backup semantics, or operational controls; always run compatibility assessments and tests against the target cluster.
improvements: Explicitly state on the product overview and quickstarts: 'Azure DocumentDB runs the open-source DocumentDB engine (link), not a mongod process or the original Cosmos DB storage engine; use Mongo drivers but test admin and migration scenarios.'

confusions.question: What database name should the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named sample_healthcare_20 for all sample collections and indexes (do not touch other databases).
confusions.grounded_answer: Verified from the sample run environment description: the sample must use the database named 'sample_healthcare_20'.

confusions.question: What vector index definition does this sample need for vector search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a knn vector index on the providers collection embedding field. Example Mongo shell command: db.providers.createIndex( { embedding: 'knnVector' }, { name: 'vec_idx', knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } } ) — change dimensions to match your embedding model.
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong syntax for Azure DocumentDB: create the vector index using DocumentDB's createIndexes / createSearchIndexes semantics and cosmosSearchOptions with kind set to 'vector-hnsw','vector-ivf' or 'vector-diskann', and dimensions matching the embedding model. Example: an HNSW index JSON with cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } and then query with $search using the cosmosSearch operator.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer used Atlas/knnVector createIndex syntax rather than DocumentDB's cosmosSearchOptions/createIndexes shape.
confusions.build_risk: Using Atlas syntax will fail; the sample's seed/index creation script must use DocumentDB createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions so the vector index is created and queries work.
improvements: Provide one copy-pasteable createIndexes JSON for HNSW and one for DiskANN in the sample's seed/index script README and call the documentdb.create_index MCP tool or pymongo command that wraps this JSON.

confusions.question: What exact connection code will the sample use at runtime to open a client?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient. Example Python: import os from pymongo import MongoClient client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000) db = client['sample_healthcare_20']
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: docs and the run environment expect the builder to read DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient (with sensible options such as serverSelectionTimeoutMS and maxIdleTimeMS to handle pooled connections). The documentdb-driver skill recommends a process-wide singleton MongoClient and connection tuning.

confusions.question: Which Python library will the sample use to talk to the DB and to store vectors?
confusions.cold_answer: Use pymongo for MongoDB-compatible operations (pip install pymongo). Store vectors as a numeric array field e.g. 'embedding': [0.123, 0.456, ...] and use the createIndex command above to create the vector index. For LlamaIndex integration, generate embeddings with your embedding model and insert documents with that embedding field.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: pymongo is the recommended data-plane driver; vectors are stored as number[] in a field (e.g., 'embedding'). The vector indexing and queries use the cosmosSearch index and $search aggregation as documented. LlamaIndex/embedding code runs client-side to produce the numeric arrays to insert.

confusions.question: Which authentication credential will the sample use for data-plane access?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the account primary connection string (username and primary key) placed in the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable for data-plane access; Azure AD-based driver auth is not used for this sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct: using the account connection string (username/password) in DOCUMENTDB_URI is a valid and common approach and matches the run environment. However the service also supports Microsoft Entra ID/OIDC for data-plane authentication when enabled; the sample should document the default (DOCUMENTDB_URI) approach and optionally document how to enable Entra ID if the author prefers managed identity flows.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed only username/password flows. The service docs show Entra ID is an option and can (and often should) be used for better security posture.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes only primary-keys, it may encourage embedding long-lived secrets; recommend documenting Entra ID flows and how to enable them as an alternative.
improvements: In the sample README, explicitly document the default (DOCUMENTDB_URI with primary key) plus an 'Optional' section showing steps to enable Microsoft Entra ID and how to construct an OIDC connection string.

information_gaps.title: Embedding model & dimensions
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't state which embedding model/provider to use (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, text-embedding-3-large, private model). This determines vector dimensions (e.g., 1536) and index parameters. I checked the DocumentDB vector-search docs and LangChain/LlamaIndex integrations but found no single recommended model — the builder must pick one and ensure index dimensions match. Looked at learn.microsoft.com vector-search and build-rag docs.

information_gaps.title: Embedding provider credentials env var name
information_gaps.description: The run environment supplies DOCUMENTDB_URI but doesn't name the environment variable for embedding/LLM provider credentials (OPENAI_API_KEY or a different name). I searched the prompt and installed skills; none set a canonical env var name for the sample's embedding provider. The builder must choose and document it (common choice: OPENAI_API_KEY).

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset content & idempotency
information_gaps.description: Prompt doesn't include a sample dataset nor seed script idempotency rules. The documentdb-local-deployment skill explains seed patterns but does not supply the actual sample data. The builder must decide sample size, content, and make the seed script idempotent. I inspected the documentdb-local-deployment skill description but found no sample dataset.

information_gaps.title: Index method choice & tuning for sample scale
information_gaps.description: The docs describe vector index types (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) and tuning knobs, but do not recommend exact parameters for a small (10–100 record) sample. The builder must choose defaults (HNSW with small dims/parameters or IVF with numLists=1 for demo); I reviewed vector-search docs but they leave tuning choices to workload size.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore MongoDB clusters, not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; author IaC examples (Bicep or Terraform) and CLI snippets in the sample README that call mongoClusters. Grounding: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters template pages.

Create vector indexes using DocumentDB's cosmosSearch/createIndexes form (kinds: vector-hnsw/vector-ivf/vector-diskann) and query with $search + cosmosSearch, not Atlas knnVector syntax. Include example createIndexes JSON in the seed script and call it via the documentdb MCP tool or pymongo. Grounding: DocumentDB vector-search quickstart.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH so builders can run interactive connectivity and index checks (e.g., 'mongosh "mongodb+srv://<cluster>..."'). On macOS/homebrew: 'brew install mongosh' or get from MongoDB downloads. If not added, instruct the agent kit to use the documentdb MCP tools for all data-plane checks.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install Bicep if the sample repository wants to include/validate Bicep IaC locally. Easiest: 'az bicep install' via the Azure CLI. If not available, document how to build Bicep in CI or use the template JSON directly.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install Terraform only if the repo provides Terraform IaC to validate locally. Otherwise the builder can produce Terraform files but rely on CI or another machine to run 'terraform init/plan'.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: azd is helpful for template-based app scaffolding, but is not required for a single-service Python sample that uses an existing cluster. Add only if you plan to include azd-driven deploy examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python sample. Only add dotnet if the repo includes .NET example code or Function trigger examples.
